chapter.title: Fetching a page and keeping a copy

cards.body: Your clipper does not just read the rival's pricing page and bin the paper. **They cut the page out and drop it in a folder labelled with today's date.** Picture a filing cabinet with one drawer per morning. Tomorrow they pull two clippings, lay them side by side on the desk, and the difference jumps out.
cards.simpler: Imagine someone whose job is to check a rival's pricing page every morning. They do not just read it and throw the paper away. **They cut the page out and put it in a folder marked with today's date.** Think of a filing cabinet with one drawer for each morning. The next day they take out two clippings and lay them side by side. Any change is easy to spot.

cards.prompt: Monday, your clipper reads a rival's pricing page, shrugs, and bins it. Tuesday they read it again: the Pro plan is $29. Was it $29 on Monday too?

options.text: No way to know. Monday's page is in the bin.
Yes, if the clipper remembers it that way.

whyNot.a: That's a guess, not a check: pricing pages change quietly, and the whole point of the agent is to notice when they do.
whyNot.c: That's memory, not a copy: the agent has no memory between runs unless you save one to disk.

cards.reteach: The agent runs fresh each day and forgets everything from the day before. The only way it can know what a page used to say is if yesterday's run saved a copy. No saved copy, no comparison, no 'what changed'.

cards.title: Fetching is downloading the words
cards.body:
*Fetching* a page means asking a web address for its content and getting the text back, the same thing your browser does before it draws anything. A tool called *curl* (a one-line command that downloads a web address) does this, and so do a few lines of Python.

What comes back is *HTML*, the code behind a web page. It is noisy: tags, scripts, styling. The words a human reads are buried inside.

**Your only job on this step is to get those words onto your own disk.** Not to understand them, not to tidy them. Just to keep them.
cards.simpler: Fetching a page means asking a web address for its content and getting the text back. Your browser does this before it draws anything. A small tool called curl, one typed command, can do it. So can a few lines of Python. What comes back is HTML, the code behind a web page. It is messy, and the readable words are buried inside. **Your only job here is to save those words on your own computer.** Nothing more.

cards.title: 1,400 lines of purple buttons
cards.body:
Say on 4 October you fetch a rival's pricing page with one command: curl https://example.com/pricing > 2026-10-04-pricing.txt

You open the file. It is 48 kilobytes, about 1,400 lines. Roughly 20 of those lines are words a person would read: plan names, three prices, a line about a free trial. The other 1,380 exist mostly to make a button purple.

That is fine. **The three prices are in there**, and tomorrow you will have a second file to hold up next to this one.
cards.simpler: Say on 4 October you grab a rival's pricing page with one command: curl https://example.com/pricing > 2026-10-04-pricing.txt. You open the file. It is 48 kilobytes, about 1,400 lines. Only about 20 lines are words a person would read: plan names, three prices, a note about a free trial. The other 1,380 lines exist mostly to make a button purple. That is fine. **The three prices are in there.** Tomorrow you will have a second file to set beside it.

cards.prompt: You're writing the fetch step for a rival called Acme. Which file name do you save to?

options.text: acme-pricing.txt, overwritten every run so it's always current
acme-pricing-latest.txt, and you remember the old price in your head

whyNot.a: That's today's copy replacing yesterday's: once it's overwritten, there is nothing left to compare against.
whyNot.c: That's your memory doing the agent's job: the agent cannot read your head, and by day 8 neither can you.

cards.reteach: Put the date at the front of the file name, year first, like 2026-10-04. Each run then adds a new file instead of replacing the old one, and the files sort in date order on their own. Yesterday's copy stays untouched, which is the whole reason you saved it.

cards.title: A photo, not a window
cards.body:
A fetched page is a *snapshot*: a photo of the page at one moment. It is not a live window. If the site changes an hour later, your file does not. **A photo you kept is the only past the agent has.**

Keep one file per page per day, date first in the name, in a folder per competitor. Seven days in, you have seven photos of one page in a row.

One more habit: open the file after each fetch. A blocked request saves a file too, but it says 'Access denied' instead of prices. A 2-second look catches that.
cards.simpler: A fetched page is a snapshot, a photo of the page at one moment, not a live window. If the site changes later, your file does not. **That saved photo is the only past the agent has.** Keep one file per page per day, date first in the name, one folder per competitor. Then open each file after fetching. A blocked request still saves a file, but it says 'Access denied' instead of prices. A quick look catches that.

cards.body: Priya set up her fetch on a Monday, named the file pricing.txt, and let it run nightly. The following Tuesday a colleague asked when the rival's price went up. She opened her folder: one file, today's page, no history. **Eight runs had produced one copy.** The tell is simple: if the folder does not grow by one file per day, you are overwriting, not keeping.
cards.simpler: Priya set up her fetch on a Monday. She named the file pricing.txt and let it run every night. The next Tuesday a colleague asked when the rival's price had gone up. She opened her folder and found one file: today's page, no history. **Eight runs had produced one copy.** Each night had written over the night before. The warning sign is easy: if the folder does not gain one new file each day, you are overwriting, not keeping.

cards.prompt: Your agent fetched 5 pages this morning. Why save them to disk at all, instead of handing them straight to the model?

options.text: Saving makes the model read them faster.
Tomorrow's run needs today's copies to compare against.
Websites require a saved copy before they let you fetch again.

whyNot.a: That's speed, not memory: the model reads at the same pace either way, and today's copy is for tomorrow, not for the model.
whyNot.c: That's made-up etiquette: sites don't know or care what you keep; you keep copies for yourself.

cards.reteach: Think of the clipper's folder. Today's clipping is boring on its own. It only earns its place tomorrow, when the next one lands beside it and the two can be compared. Save today so tomorrow has a yesterday.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Fetch each page as text and save it in a file named with today's date, so tomorrow's copy has something to sit next to.** The agent has no memory between runs; the folder of dated files is its memory.
cards.simpler: **Fetch each page as text and save it in a file named with today's date, so tomorrow's copy has something to sit next to.** The agent forgets everything between runs. It starts each time with a blank mind. The folder of dated files is its memory. Like a diary, each day gets its own page, and the pages together tell the story.

cards.body: Open a terminal and run curl on one competitor page, saving to a file named with today's date, like 2026-10-04-pricing.txt. Open the file and search for one word you know is on the page.
cards.simpler: Open a terminal, the window where you type commands. Run curl on one competitor's page and save the result to a file named with today's date, such as 2026-10-04-pricing.txt. Then open that file. **Search inside it for one word you know is on the page**, like a plan name or a price. If you find it, the fetch worked and you have your first dated copy.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now fetch one competitor page, save it as a dated text file, and open it to check the words are really there.
